text: Education begins with stories, since children hear stories before they ever train their bodies (Republic 376e–377a), and the founders of the city must therefore supervise the makers of stories. Socrates lays down two laws governing what may be said about the gods. The first is that God is good, and for that reason the cause of good things only (379b–c). The evils in the world far outnumber the goods, and some cause other than God must be found for them, because nothing good can harm. The second law is that God neither changes nor deceives (380d–383a). Whatever is in the best condition is least altered by outside forces, and a perfect being would never willingly change itself for the worse. These two laws exclude a large part of the inherited poetry: Homer's two jars standing at the threshold of Zeus (379d), every poet who blames a god for the ruin of a household, and every shape-shifting god of the old stories. On deception Socrates adds a distinction. The lie that gods and human beings hate most is the lie in the soul, which is worse than the lie spoken aloud. It is the condition of being deceived about reality in the most important part of oneself (382a–b). A god has no such lie within, and no motive to put one in anyone else.
